paragraphs: You know, my dears, that your mother was an orphan and an only child. I daresay you have heard that your grandfather was a clergyman up in Westmoreland, where I come from. I was only a girl at the village school when, one day, your grandmother came to ask the teacher whether any of her pupils would make a suitable nursery maid. I can tell you how proud I was when the teacher called me forward and described me as a good needleworker, a reliable, honest girl whose parents were very respectable, even if they were poor. I thought nothing could please me more than serving this pretty young lady. She blushed as deeply as I did while she spoke about the coming baby and what I would have to do for it. But I can see that this part of my story interests you less than what you think is coming, so I will get on. I was hired and settled in the parsonage before Miss Rosamond was born—that was the baby who is now your mother. To be sure, I had little enough to do for her at first. She was never out of her mother’s arms and slept beside her all night. How proud I was on the occasions when my mistress trusted her to me! There was never such a baby before or since, though you have all been fine enough babies in your turn. But none of you has matched your mother’s sweet, winning ways. She took after her own mother, who was a lady by birth: a Miss Furnivall, granddaughter of Lord Furnivall in Northumberland. I believe she had no brothers or sisters. She had been brought up in my lord’s family until she married your grandfather. He was only a curate, the son of a Carlisle shopkeeper, but as clever and fine a gentleman as ever lived. He worked extremely hard in his parish, which was very large and scattered far and wide over the Westmoreland Fells. When your mother, little Miss Rosamond, was about four or five, both her parents died within a fortnight, one after the other. Ah, that was a sad time! My pretty young mistress and I were waiting for another baby to be born when my master came home wet and tired from one of his long rides and caught the fever that killed him. After that, she never raised her head again. She lived just long enough to see her dead baby and have it laid on her breast before she breathed her life away. On her deathbed, my mistress asked me never to leave Miss Rosamond. But even if she had said nothing, I would have followed that little child to the end of the world.

Before our sobbing had properly stopped, the executors and guardians arrived to settle the affairs. They were my poor young mistress’s own cousin, Lord Furnivall, and my master’s brother, Mr. Esthwaite, a Manchester shopkeeper. He was not then as well off as he later became, and he had a large, growing family. Well, I don’t know whether it was their decision or the result of a letter my mistress wrote to her cousin, my lord, from her deathbed. Somehow it was settled that Miss Rosamond and I would go to Furnivall Manor House in Northumberland. My lord spoke as though her mother had wished her to live with his family, and as though he had no objection, since one or two extra people could make no difference to such a grand household. That was not how I would have wished my bright, pretty pet’s arrival to be regarded. She was like a sunbeam in any family, however grand! Still, I was very pleased by the way everyone in the Dale stared and admired when they heard I was going to be a young lady’s maid at Lord Furnivall’s, at Furnivall Manor.

But I was mistaken in thinking we were going to live where my lord did. It turned out that the family had left Furnivall Manor House fifty years or more before. I could find no account of my poor young mistress ever having been there, although she had grown up in the family. That saddened me, for I would have liked Miss Rosamond to spend her childhood where her mother had spent hers.

I asked my lord’s personal servant as many questions as I dared. He said the Manor House stood at the foot of the Cumberland Fells and was a very grand place. An elderly Miss Furnivall, my lord’s great-aunt, lived there with only a few servants. But it was a very healthy place, and my lord thought it would suit Miss Rosamond well for a few years. Perhaps having her there would also amuse his old aunt.

My lord ordered me to have Miss Rosamond’s things ready by a certain day. He was a stern, proud man, as all the Lords Furnivall were said to be, and never spoke more than necessary. People said he had loved my young mistress. But knowing his father would object, she would not listen to him and married Mr. Esthwaite instead. I don’t know whether that is true. At any rate, he never married. Yet he took little notice of Miss Rosamond, which I thought he might have done if he had cared for her dead mother. He sent his personal servant with us to the Manor House and told him to join him in Newcastle that same evening. So the man had little time to introduce us to all the strangers before he, too, got rid of us. We were left, two lonely young things—I was not yet eighteen—in the great old Manor House. Our drive there seems like yesterday. We had left our own dear parsonage very early, both crying as though our hearts would break, even though we were travelling in my lord’s carriage, which I had once thought so grand. Now it was long past noon on a September day. We stopped to change horses for the last time in a little smoky town full of coal workers and miners. Miss Rosamond had fallen asleep, but Mr. Henry told me to wake her so that she could see the park and the Manor House as we drove up. I thought it a pity, but did as he said for fear he would complain about me to my lord. We had left every sign of a town, or even a village, behind and passed through the gates of a large, wild park. It was nothing like the parks here in the south. There were rocks, the sound of running water, gnarled thorn trees, and old oaks, white and stripped of bark with age.

The road climbed for about two miles before we saw a great, stately house. Trees crowded around it so closely that, in places, their branches dragged against the walls when the wind blew. Some hung broken. No one seemed to care much for the place by trimming the trees or tending the moss-covered carriage drive. Only the space in front of the house was clear. The great oval drive had not a weed in it, and neither tree nor climbing plant was allowed to grow over the long front with its many windows. A wing projected at either end, each forming the end of one of the house’s side fronts. Desolate though it was, the house was even grander than I had expected. Behind it rose the Fells, bare and apparently unenclosed. To the left as you faced the house was a little old-fashioned flower garden, as I later discovered. A door opened onto it from the west front. It had been hollowed out of the thick, dark woods for some Lady Furnivall of long ago. But the great woodland trees had spread their branches over it again, and very few flowers could live in its shade by then.

When we drove up to the main entrance and went into the hall, I thought we would get lost, it was so large and vast and grand. An entirely bronze chandelier hung from the middle of the ceiling. I had never seen one before and stared at it in amazement. At one end of the hall stood a fireplace as big as the sides of houses where I came from, with massive iron stands to support the logs. Beside it were heavy, old-fashioned sofas. At the opposite end, on your left as you entered—the western side—an organ was built into the wall, so large that it filled most of that end of the hall. Beyond it, on the same side, was a door. Opposite, on either side of the fireplace, doors led into the east front. But I never passed through those for as long as I stayed in the house, so I cannot tell you what lay beyond.

The afternoon was drawing to an end. With no fire lit, the hall looked dark and gloomy, but we did not remain there a moment. The old servant who had opened the door bowed to Mr. Henry and led us through the doorway beyond the great organ. We followed him through several smaller halls and passages to the west drawing room, where he said Miss Furnivall was sitting. Poor little Miss Rosamond clung tightly to me, as though frightened and lost in that enormous place. I felt little better myself. The west drawing room looked very cheerful, with a warm fire and plenty of good, comfortable furniture. Miss Furnivall was an old lady of almost eighty, I should think, though I do not know. She was tall and thin, her face covered in fine wrinkles as though someone had drawn them with the point of a needle. Her eyes were very watchful, perhaps to make up for her hearing: she was so deaf that she had to use an ear trumpet. Beside her, working on the same large piece of tapestry, sat Mrs. Stark, her maid and companion, almost as old as she was. Mrs. Stark had lived with Miss Furnivall since they were both young and now seemed more a friend than a servant. She looked cold, grey, and stony, as though she had never loved or cared about anyone. I don’t suppose she cared for anyone except her mistress. Because Miss Furnivall was so deaf, Mrs. Stark treated her very much like a child. Mr. Henry delivered some message from my lord, then bowed goodbye to everyone. He ignored my sweet little Miss Rosamond’s outstretched hand and left us standing there while the two old ladies examined us through their spectacles.

I was very glad when they rang for the old footman who had first shown us in and told him to take us to our rooms. We left the great drawing room, passed through another sitting room, and climbed a broad flight of stairs. Then we went along a wide gallery, rather like a library, with books all along one side and windows and writing tables along the other. At last, we reached our rooms. I was pleased to hear they stood directly above the kitchens, for I was beginning to fear losing myself in that wilderness of a house. There was an old nursery, once used by all the little lords and ladies, with a pleasant fire in the grate, a kettle boiling beside it on the hob, and tea things laid out on the table. Opening off it was the sleeping nursery, with a little cot for Miss Rosamond close to my bed. Old James called his wife, Dorothy, upstairs to welcome us. They were both so hospitable and kind that, before long, Miss Rosamond and I felt quite at home. By the end of tea, she was sitting on Dorothy’s knee, chattering as fast as her little tongue could go. I soon discovered that Dorothy came from Westmoreland, which formed a bond between us. I would never wish to meet kinder people than old James and his wife. James had lived in my lord’s family for almost his whole life and thought no one else was so grand. He even looked down a little on his wife, because before marrying him she had lived only in a farmer’s household. But he was very fond of her, as well he might be. They had one servant under them to do all the hard work, a girl called Agnes. She and I, James and Dorothy, Miss Furnivall and Mrs. Stark made up the household—always remembering my sweet little Miss Rosamond! I often wondered how they had managed before she came, they thought so much of her now. It was the same in the kitchen and the drawing room. Stern, sad Miss Furnivall and cold Mrs. Stark looked pleased when she fluttered in like a bird, playing and darting here and there, with a constant murmur and sweet chatter of happiness. I am sure they were often sorry when she flitted away into the kitchen, though they were too proud to ask her to stay and a little surprised at her preference. Still, as Mrs. Stark said, it was hardly surprising when one remembered the stock her father came from. The great old rambling house was a wonderful place for little Miss Rosamond. She explored it everywhere, with me at her heels—everywhere except the east wing, which was never opened and which we never thought of entering. But the western and northern parts contained many pleasant rooms full of things that seemed curious to us, although they might not have to people who had seen more of the world. Sweeping tree branches and overgrown ivy darkened the windows. Yet in the green gloom we could make out old china jars, carved ivory boxes, great heavy books, and, above all, the old pictures!

Once, I remember, my darling insisted that Dorothy come with us to tell us who the people in the pictures were. They were all portraits of my lord’s family, though Dorothy did not know every name. We had been through most of the rooms when we reached the old formal drawing room above the hall. There was a portrait of Miss Furnivall—or Miss Grace, as she had been called then, being the younger sister. What a beauty she must have been! Yet her face was so fixed and proud, with such scorn in her handsome eyes. Her eyebrows were slightly raised, as though she wondered how anyone could dare to look at her, and her lip curled at us as we stood gazing. I had never seen clothes like hers, though they had been the height of fashion in her youth. A hat of soft white material, rather like beaver felt, was pulled slightly over her brows, with a beautiful plume of feathers sweeping around one side. Her blue satin gown opened at the front over a quilted white panel across her bodice.
“Well, goodness!” I said when I had looked my fill. “They say flesh is like grass. But looking at Miss Furnivall now, who would have thought she had been such a complete beauty?”

“Yes,” Dorothy said. “People change sadly. But if what my master’s father used to say was true, Miss Furnivall, the elder sister, was even more beautiful than Miss Grace. Her picture is somewhere here. But if I show you, you must never let anyone know—not even James—that you have seen it. Do you think the little lady can keep quiet?” she asked.

I was not so sure, for she was such a sweet, bold, open little child. So I told her to go and hide. Then I helped Dorothy turn around a large picture that stood leaning with its face to the wall, instead of hanging like the others. It certainly surpassed Miss Grace’s portrait for beauty and, I think, for scornful pride too, though that was harder to judge. I could have looked at it for an hour. But Dorothy seemed half frightened that she had shown it to me. She hurriedly turned it back and told me to run and find Miss Rosamond, because there were some unpleasant places in the house where she would not like the child to go. I was a brave, high-spirited girl and paid little attention to what she said. I enjoyed hide-and-seek as much as any child in the parish, so off I ran to find my little one.

As winter approached and the days shortened, I sometimes felt almost certain I could hear a sound like someone playing the great organ in the hall. I did not hear it every evening, but certainly very often. It was usually when I was sitting with Miss Rosamond after putting her to bed, keeping perfectly still and silent in the bedroom. Then I would hear it booming and swelling in the distance. The first night, when I went downstairs for supper, I asked Dorothy who had been playing. James snapped that I was a fool to mistake the wind sighing through the trees for music. But I saw Dorothy look at him very fearfully, and Bessy, the kitchen maid, muttered something under her breath and turned quite white. They clearly disliked my question, so I kept quiet until I could be alone with Dorothy. Then I knew I could get a good deal out of her. The next day, I watched for my chance and coaxed her to tell me who played the organ. Despite keeping quiet in front of James, I knew perfectly well it was the organ, not the wind. But Dorothy had been told what to say, I’m sure, and I could not get a word out of her. Then I tried Bessy, although I had always considered myself a little above her. I was on the same footing as James and Dorothy, while she was hardly more than their servant. She told me I must never, never tell; and if I ever did, I must never say she had told me. But it was a very strange noise. She had heard it many times, especially on winter nights and before storms. People said it was the old lord playing the great organ in the hall, just as he had when he was alive. But who the old lord was, why he played, and why especially on stormy winter evenings, she either could not or would not tell me. Well, I have told you I had a brave heart. I thought it rather pleasant to hear that grand music rolling through the house, whoever was playing. It would rise above the great gusts of wind, wailing and triumphing like a living creature, then fall to the gentlest softness. But it was always music, always tunes, so calling it the wind was nonsense. At first, I thought Miss Furnivall might be playing without Bessy knowing. But one day, alone in the hall, I opened the organ and peered all through and around it, as I had once done with the organ in Crosthwaite church. Inside, it was all broken and destroyed, though it looked so fine and magnificent outside. Then, although it was midday, my skin began to crawl a little. I closed it and ran quite quickly back to my own bright nursery. For some time afterwards, I disliked hearing the music as much as James and Dorothy did. Meanwhile, everyone grew fonder and fonder of Miss Rosamond. The old ladies liked her to join them for their early dinner. James stood behind Miss Furnivall’s chair and I behind Miss Rosamond’s, with great ceremony. Afterwards, she would play as quietly as a mouse in a corner of the big drawing room while Miss Furnivall slept and I ate my dinner in the kitchen. But she was glad enough to join me in the nursery later. As she said, Miss Furnivall was so sad and Mrs. Stark so dull. She and I were merry enough, though, and in time I stopped worrying about the strange rolling music. It did no one any harm, even if we did not know where it came from.

That winter was very cold. The frosts began in the middle of October and lasted many, many weeks. One day at dinner, I remember Miss Furnivall raising her sad, heavy eyes and saying to Mrs. Stark, “I am afraid we shall have a terrible winter,” in a strange, meaningful way. Mrs. Stark pretended not to hear and talked loudly about something else. My little lady and I did not mind the frost—not we! As long as it stayed dry, we climbed the steep slopes behind the house and went up onto the bleak, bare Fells. We raced each other in the fresh, sharp air. Once, we came down by a new path that took us past two old, gnarled holly trees growing about halfway down beside the east side of the house. But the days grew shorter and shorter. The old lord, if it was he, kept playing the great organ more and more stormily and sadly. One Sunday afternoon, which must have been towards the end of November, I asked Dorothy to take charge of little missy when she left the drawing room after Miss Furnivall’s nap. It was too cold to take her to church with me, but I wanted to go. Dorothy gladly promised. She loved the child so much that everything seemed safely arranged. Bessy and I set off briskly, although the sky hung heavy and black over the white earth, as though night had never quite left it. The air was still, but bitingly cold.

“We’ll have snow,” Bessy told me. Sure enough, while we were in church it began to fall in great, thick flakes, so thick they almost darkened the windows. It had stopped before we came out, but lay soft, deep, and thick beneath our feet as we trudged home. The moon rose before we reached the house. Between the moonlight and the dazzling white snow, I think it was lighter then than when we had gone to church between two and three o’clock. I have not told you that Miss Furnivall and Mrs. Stark never went to church. They read the prayers together in their quiet, gloomy way. Sundays seemed very long to them without their tapestry to keep them busy. So when I went to Dorothy in the kitchen to collect Miss Rosamond and take her upstairs, I was not very surprised to hear that the ladies had kept her. She had never come to the kitchen, as I had told her to do when she tired of behaving nicely in the drawing room. I took off my outdoor things and went to find her and bring her to supper in the nursery. But in the main drawing room sat the two old ladies, very still and quiet, saying a word now and then. They looked as though nothing as bright and merry as Miss Rosamond had ever been near them. Still, I thought she might be hiding from me. It was one of her sweet little ways. Perhaps she had persuaded them to pretend they knew nothing about her. So I crept about, peeping under a sofa here and behind a chair there, pretending to be terribly frightened because I could not find her.

“What is the matter, Hester?” Mrs. Stark asked sharply. I don’t know whether Miss Furnivall had seen me. As I told you, she was very deaf, and she sat perfectly still, staring idly into the fire with her hopeless face. “I’m only looking for my little Rosy Posy,” I replied, still believing the child was there, close to me, though I could not see her.
“Miss Rosamond is not here,” Mrs. Stark said. “She went to find Dorothy more than an hour ago.” She too turned back to the fire.

My heart sank, and I began to wish I had never left my darling. I went back and told Dorothy. James had gone out for the day, but Dorothy, Bessy, and I took lights and went upstairs to the nursery first. Then we searched through the great, enormous house, calling and begging Miss Rosamond to come out of her hiding place and stop frightening us to death. But there was no answer, no sound.
“Oh!” I said at last. “Could she have got into the east wing and hidden there?”

Dorothy said that was impossible. She had never been in there herself. The doors were always locked, and she believed my lord’s steward kept the keys. At any rate, neither she nor James had ever seen them. I said I would go back and see whether the child was hidden in the drawing room after all, without the old ladies knowing. If I found her there, I said, I would give her a good whipping for the fright she had given me. But I never meant to do it. Back I went to the west drawing room and told Mrs. Stark we could not find her anywhere. I asked permission to search around all the furniture, thinking she might have fallen asleep in a warm, hidden corner. But no! We searched—Miss Furnivall got up and searched, trembling all over—and she was nowhere there. Then everyone in the house set off again and looked in all the places we had already searched, but we could not find her. Miss Furnivall shivered and shook so much that Mrs. Stark took her back to the warm drawing room. Before going, they made me promise to bring the child to them once she was found. Oh, dear! I was beginning to think she would never be found when I thought of looking into the great front courtyard, covered in snow. I was upstairs when I looked out. The moonlight was so clear that I could plainly see the prints of two little feet, leading from the hall door around the corner of the east wing. I don’t know how I got downstairs. I tugged the great, stiff hall door open, threw my gown’s skirt over my head as a cloak, and ran outside. Around the east corner, a black shadow fell over the snow. But when I reached the moonlight again, there were the little footprints, going up—up towards the Fells. It was bitterly cold, so cold the air almost stripped the skin from my face as I ran. But on I ran, crying at the thought of how frozen and frightened my poor little darling must be. I was within sight of the holly trees when I saw a shepherd coming down the hill with something in his arms, wrapped in his woollen shawl. He shouted to ask whether I had lost a child. I was crying too hard to speak. He came towards me, and I saw my tiny little one lying still, white, and stiff in his arms, as though dead. He told me he had been up on the Fells to gather his sheep before the deep cold of night. Under the holly trees—black marks on the hillside, with no other bushes for miles—he had found my little lady, my lamb, my queen, my darling, cold and stiff in that terrible sleep brought on by frost. Oh, the joy and tears of holding her in my arms again! I would not let him carry her. I took her, shawl and all, into my own arms and held her close to my warm neck and heart. I felt life slowly returning to her gentle little limbs. But she was still unconscious when we reached the house, and I had no breath to speak. We went in through the kitchen door.

“Bring me the warming pan for the bed,” I said. I carried her upstairs and began undressing her beside the nursery fire, which Bessy had kept burning. With tears blinding my eyes, I called my little lamb every sweet, playful name I could think of. At last—oh, at last!—she opened her large blue eyes. Then I put her into her warm bed and sent Dorothy downstairs to tell Miss Furnivall that all was well. I resolved to sit beside my darling’s bed the whole long night. As soon as her pretty head touched the pillow, she slipped into a gentle sleep. I watched over her until morning, when she woke bright and clear—or so I thought at first. And, my dears, that is what I think now.

She said she had wanted to go to Dorothy because both old ladies were asleep and the drawing room was very dull. Passing through the west lobby, she had looked through the high window and seen snow falling—falling softly and steadily. But she wanted to see it lying pretty and white on the ground, so she went into the great hall. At the window there, she saw it bright and soft on the drive. As she stood there, she saw a little girl younger than herself. “But so pretty,” my darling said. “And the little girl beckoned me to come out. Oh, she was so pretty and so sweet, I couldn’t help going.” Then the other little girl had taken her hand, and together they had gone around the east corner.

“Now you are being a naughty little girl and telling lies,” I said. “What would your good mamma say to her little Rosamond? She is in heaven and never told a lie in her life. What would she say if she heard you telling lies—and I daresay she does hear you!”
“Really, Hester,” my child sobbed, “I am telling you the truth. I really am.”

“Don’t tell me that!” I said very sternly. “I followed your footprints in the snow. There were only yours. If a little girl had walked hand in hand with you up the hill, don’t you think her footprints would have been beside yours?”

“I can’t help it, dear, dear Hester, if they weren’t,” she said, crying. “I never looked at her feet. But she held my hand firmly and tightly in her little one, and it was very, very cold. She took me up the path on the Fell to the holly trees. There I saw a lady weeping and crying. But when she saw me, she stopped crying and gave a very proud, grand smile. She took me on her knee and began to lull me to sleep. That’s all, Hester, but it is true, and my dear mamma knows it is.” She was crying. I thought she must have a fever and pretended to believe her as she repeated her story over and over, always the same. At last, Dorothy knocked with Miss Rosamond’s breakfast. She told me the old ladies were downstairs in the dining room and wanted to speak to me. Both had come into the sleeping nursery the evening before, but Miss Rosamond was already asleep. They had only looked at her, without asking me any questions.

“I’m going to be told off,” I thought as I went along the north gallery. Then I took courage. “But I left her in their charge. They are to blame for letting her slip away without anyone noticing or watching.” So I went in boldly and told my story. I shouted the whole thing close to Miss Furnivall’s ear. But when I mentioned the other little girl in the snow, coaxing and tempting Rosamond outside and drawing her up towards the grand, beautiful lady by the holly tree, Miss Furnivall flung up her arms—her old, withered arms—and cried, “Oh, Heaven, forgive! Have mercy!”
Mrs. Stark took hold of her, rather roughly, I thought. But Miss Furnivall was beyond her control and spoke to me with a sort of wild warning and authority.

“Hester! Keep her away from that child! It will lure her to her death! That evil child! Tell her it is a wicked, naughty child.” Then Mrs. Stark hurried me out of the room. I was glad enough to leave. But Miss Furnivall went on shrieking, “Oh, have mercy! Will You never forgive? It was many long years ago—”

After that, I was deeply uneasy. I never dared leave Miss Rosamond, night or day, for fear she would slip away again after some fancy or other. I was all the more worried because, from everyone’s odd behaviour around Miss Furnivall, I thought I could see that she was mad. I feared that something similar might threaten my darling—it might run in the family, you know. All this time, the hard frost continued without a break. On nights stormier than usual, we heard the old lord playing the great organ between the gusts and through the wind. But old lord or not, I followed wherever Miss Rosamond went. My love for that pretty, helpless orphan was stronger than my fear of the grand, terrible sound. Besides, it was my responsibility to keep her cheerful and happy, as a child her age should be. So we played together and wandered together, here, there, and everywhere. I never again dared lose sight of her in that large, rambling house. One afternoon, not long before Christmas Day, we were playing on the billiard table in the great hall. We did not know how to play properly, but she liked rolling the smooth ivory balls with her pretty hands, and I liked doing whatever she did. Without our noticing, it grew dim indoors, although it was still light outside. I was thinking of taking her back to the nursery when she suddenly cried out,
“Look, Hester! Look! There is my poor little girl out in the snow!”

I turned towards the long, narrow windows. Sure enough, there stood a little girl smaller than Miss Rosamond, dressed quite unsuitably for being outside on such a bitter night. She was crying and beating against the windowpanes as though she wanted to be let in. She seemed to sob and wail until Miss Rosamond could bear it no longer and flew towards the door to open it. Suddenly, close beside us, the great organ thundered out so loudly that I trembled. All the more so when I remembered that, even in the stillness of that deathly cold weather, I had heard no little hands beating against the glass, although the ghost child seemed to be using all its strength. I had seen it wailing and crying, yet not the faintest sound had reached my ears. Whether I remembered all this at that very moment, I cannot say. The organ had so stunned and terrified me. But I do know that I caught Miss Rosamond before she opened the hall door. I clutched her and carried her away, kicking and screaming, into the big, bright kitchen, where Dorothy and Agnes were busy making mince pies.
“What is the matter with my sweet one?” Dorothy cried as I carried in Miss Rosamond, who was sobbing as though her heart would break.

“She won’t let me open the door for my little girl to come in! She’ll die if she stays out on the Fells all night. Cruel, naughty Hester!” she said, slapping me. But she might have struck harder, for I had seen a look of ghastly terror on Dorothy’s face that made my very blood run cold.

“Shut the back kitchen door tightly and bolt it well,” she told Agnes. She said nothing more, but gave me raisins and almonds to soothe Miss Rosamond. The child went on sobbing about the little girl in the snow and would not touch any of the treats. I was thankful when she cried herself to sleep in bed. Then I slipped down to the kitchen and told Dorothy I had made up my mind. I would take my darling back to my father’s house in Applethwaite. We lived humbly there, but we lived in peace. The old lord’s organ playing had frightened me enough, I said. But now I had seen that little moaning child for myself, dressed as no child in the neighbourhood could be, beating and battering to get in, yet always without a sound or noise, and with that dark wound on its right shoulder. Miss Rosamond had recognised it as the ghost that had nearly lured her to her death, which Dorothy knew was true. I would bear it no longer.

I saw Dorothy change colour once or twice. When I had finished, she said she did not think I could take Miss Rosamond with me. The child was my lord’s ward, and I had no rights over her. Would I leave the child I loved so much, she asked, merely because of sounds and sights that could not harm me, and that they had all had to get used to in their turn? I was hot and trembling with anger. It was all very well for her to talk, I said. She knew what these sights and sounds meant and perhaps had even had something to do with the ghost child while it was alive. I taunted her so much that she finally told me everything she knew. Then I wished she had never told me, because it only frightened me more.

She said she had heard the story from old neighbours who were still alive when she first married. In those days, people still sometimes came to the house, before it had acquired such a bad name in the surrounding countryside. What she had been told might be true, or it might not.

The old lord was Miss Furnivall’s father—Miss Grace, as Dorothy called her, because Miss Maude was the elder and properly entitled to be called Miss Furnivall. The old lord was consumed by pride. No one had ever seen or heard of such a proud man, and his daughters took after him. No one was good enough to marry them, although they had plenty of choice. They had been the great beauties of their day, as I had seen from their portraits in the formal drawing room. But, as the old saying goes, pride comes before a fall. Those two haughty beauties fell in love with the same man, and he was no better than a foreign musician their father had brought down from London to make music with him at the Manor House. For, next to his pride, the old lord loved music above everything. He could play almost every instrument anyone had heard of. It was strange that music did not soften him. He was a fierce, grim old man who had broken his poor wife’s heart with his cruelty, or so they said. He was mad about music and would pay any sum for it. So he brought this foreigner, whose music was so beautiful that even the birds in the trees were said to stop singing to listen. Gradually, the foreign gentleman gained such a hold over the old lord that nothing would satisfy him except having the man come every year. It was this musician who had the great organ brought from Holland and assembled in the hall, where it now stood. He taught the old lord to play it. But many, many times, while Lord Furnivall thought of nothing but his fine organ and still finer music, the dark foreigner was out walking in the woods with one of the young ladies—sometimes Miss Maude, sometimes Miss Grace.

Miss Maude won the contest and carried off the prize, such as it was. She and the musician married without anyone knowing. Before his next yearly visit, she had given birth to a little girl at a farmhouse on the Moors, while her father and Miss Grace thought she was away at Doncaster Races. Being a wife and mother did not soften her at all. She remained as proud and passionate as ever, perhaps even more so, because she was jealous of Miss Grace. Her foreign husband paid a great deal of attention to her sister—just to deceive her, he told his wife. But Miss Grace gloated over Miss Maude, and Miss Maude grew fiercer and fiercer with both her husband and her sister. He could easily escape anything unpleasant and hide himself in foreign countries. That summer, he went away a month earlier than usual, half threatening never to return. Meanwhile, the little girl remained at the farmhouse. At least once every week, her mother had her horse saddled and galloped wildly over the hills to see her. For when she loved, she loved, and when she hated, she hated. The old lord went on playing—playing his organ. The servants thought the sweet music he made had soothed his dreadful temper, about which, Dorothy said, some terrible stories could be told. He was growing frail too and needed a crutch to walk. His son—the present Lord Furnivall’s father—was with the army in America, and the other son was at sea. So Miss Maude could mostly do as she pleased. She and Miss Grace became colder and more bitter towards each other every day, until they hardly spoke except in their father’s presence. The foreign musician came the following summer, but it was his last visit. Their jealousy and tempers made his life so miserable that he grew tired of it, went away, and was never heard of again. Miss Maude had always intended to acknowledge her marriage after her father’s death. Now she was a deserted wife whom no one knew to be married, with a child she dared not acknowledge, although she loved it desperately. She lived with a father she feared and a sister she hated. When the next summer passed without the dark foreigner returning, both Miss Maude and Miss Grace became gloomy and sad. They looked worn and exhausted, though as beautiful as ever. But in time, Maude brightened. Her father grew more and more frail and more completely absorbed in music. She and Miss Grace lived almost entirely apart, with separate rooms: Miss Grace on the west side and Miss Maude on the east, in those very rooms that were now locked. Maude thought she could have her little girl with her without anyone ever knowing, except those who dared not speak of it. They would have to believe her claim that it was a cottager’s child she had taken a liking to. Dorothy said all this was fairly well known. What happened next, however, was known only to Miss Grace and Mrs. Stark, who was already her maid and far more of a friend to her than her sister had ever been. But from things they heard said, the servants supposed that Miss Maude had gloated over Miss Grace and told her the truth. All the time the dark foreigner had been mocking Grace with pretended love, he had been Maude’s own husband. The colour left Miss Grace’s cheeks and lips that day and never returned. She was heard to say many times that sooner or later she would have her revenge. Mrs. Stark was always spying around the east rooms.

One terrible night, just after the New Year, the snow lay thick and deep, and flakes were still falling fast enough to blind anyone outside. A great, violent noise was heard, with the old lord’s voice above everything, cursing and swearing horribly. There were a little child’s cries and a fierce woman’s proud defiance. Then came the sound of a blow, a dead silence, and moans and wails fading away on the hillside. Afterwards, the old lord summoned all his servants. With terrible oaths and still more terrible words, he told them his daughter had disgraced herself, and that he had driven her out—her and her child. If they ever gave her help, food, or shelter, he prayed they would never enter heaven. All the while, Miss Grace stood beside him, as white and still as stone. When he finished, she gave a great sigh, as if to say her work was done and her purpose achieved. But the old lord never touched his organ again. He died within the year, and no wonder! The morning after that wild and dreadful night, shepherds coming down the Fell found Miss Maude sitting beneath the holly trees, out of her mind and smiling, cradling a dead child with a terrible mark on its right shoulder. “But that was not what killed it,” Dorothy said. “It was the frost and cold. Every wild creature was in its hole and every farm animal in its enclosure, while that child and its mother were driven out to wander on the Fells! Now you know everything. I wonder if you are less frightened now?”

I was more frightened than ever, but said I was not. I wished Miss Rosamond and I were safely out of that dreadful house for good. But I would not leave her, and I dared not take her away. Oh, how I watched and guarded her! We bolted the doors and fastened the shutters an hour or more before dark, rather than leave them open five minutes too late. But my little lady still heard that strange child crying and grieving. Nothing we could do or say stopped her wanting to go to it and let it in from the cruel wind and snow. All this time, I kept as far away from Miss Furnivall and Mrs. Stark as I could, for I feared them. I knew nothing good could surround them, with their grey, hard faces and dreamy eyes staring back into the dreadful years gone by. But even through my fear, I felt a kind of pity for Miss Furnivall, at least. Even those in the depths of hell could hardly look more hopeless than she always did. In the end, I felt so sorry for her—she never spoke a word unless it was forced out of her—that I prayed for her. I taught Miss Rosamond to pray for someone who had committed a deadly sin. But often, when she reached those words, she would listen, spring up from her knees, and say, “I hear my little girl moaning and crying so sadly. Oh, let her in, or she will die!”

One night, just after New Year’s Day had finally come, when I hoped the long winter had turned a corner, I heard the west drawing room bell ring three times. That was my signal. I would not leave Miss Rosamond alone, even though she was asleep. The old lord had been playing more wildly than ever, and I feared my darling would wake and hear the ghost child. I knew she could not see it; I had secured the windows too well for that. So I lifted her from bed, wrapped her in whatever outdoor clothes were nearest, and carried her downstairs to the drawing room. The old ladies sat at their tapestry as usual. They looked up when I entered, and Mrs. Stark asked in astonishment why I had brought Miss Rosamond out of her warm bed. I began to whisper, “Because I was afraid that while I was away, the wild child in the snow might tempt her out.” But with a glance at Miss Furnivall, she cut me short. Miss Furnivall wanted me to undo some stitches she had got wrong, which neither of them could see well enough to unpick. I laid my pretty darling on the sofa, sat down beside them on a stool, and hardened my heart against them as I heard the wind rising and howling.

Miss Rosamond slept soundly on, despite the wind. Miss Furnivall said nothing and did not turn when gusts rattled the windows. Suddenly, she sprang to her full height and raised a hand as though telling us to listen.
“I hear voices!” she said. “I hear terrible screams. I hear my father’s voice!”

At that very moment, my darling woke with a start. “My little girl is crying. Oh, how she is crying!” She tried to get up and go to her, but tangled her feet in the blanket, and I caught her up. My skin had begun to crawl at these noises that they could hear while no sound reached us. Within a minute or two, the noises came, grew rapidly, and filled our ears. We too heard voices and screams, and could no longer hear the winter wind raging outside. Mrs. Stark looked at me and I at her, but we dared not speak. Suddenly, Miss Furnivall went to the door, through the outer room and west lobby, and opened the door into the great hall. Mrs. Stark followed. I dared not remain behind, although fear almost stopped my heart. Clasping my darling tightly in my arms, I went with them. In the hall, the screams were louder than ever. They seemed to come from the east wing, nearer and nearer, just beyond the locked doors, close behind them. Then I noticed that the great bronze chandelier seemed fully lit, although the hall was dim. A fire blazed in the enormous fireplace but gave no warmth. I shuddered with terror and hugged my darling closer. As I did, the east door shook. Suddenly, she struggled to escape my arms and cried, “Hester! I must go. My little girl is there! I hear her. She is coming! Hester, I must go!”

I held her tightly with all my strength. With a fixed determination, I held her. Even if I had died, my hands would still have gripped her, so firmly had I made up my mind. Miss Furnivall stood listening and paid no attention to my darling. The child had got down to the floor. Now on my knees, I held both arms around her neck while she struggled and cried to get free.

Suddenly, the east door burst open with a thunderous crash, as though wrenched open in a violent rage. Into that broad, mysterious light came the figure of a tall old man with grey hair and gleaming eyes. With repeated, merciless gestures of disgust, he drove before him a stern, beautiful woman, with a little child clinging to her dress.

“Oh, Hester! Hester!” Miss Rosamond cried. “It’s the lady! The lady under the holly trees! My little girl is with her. Hester! Hester! Let me go to her. They are pulling me towards them. I can feel them—I can feel them. I must go!”

Again, her efforts to escape almost convulsed her. But I held her tighter and tighter, until I feared I would hurt her. Better that than let her go towards those terrible ghosts. They moved towards the great hall door, where the winds howled and hungered for their prey. Before reaching it, the lady turned. I could see her defying the old man with fierce, proud defiance. Then she shrank in fear. She flung up her arms wildly and pitifully to save her child—her little child—from a blow of his raised crutch.
Miss Rosamond was pulled as though by a power greater than mine. She writhed in my arms and sobbed, for by now the poor darling was growing faint.

“They want me to go with them onto the Fells. They are pulling me towards them. Oh, my little girl! I would come, but cruel, wicked Hester is holding me so tightly.” But when she saw the raised crutch, she fainted, and I thanked God. At that moment, the tall old man was about to strike the shrinking little child, his hair streaming as though in the blast of a furnace. Miss Furnivall, the old woman beside me, cried, “Oh, Father! Father! Spare the innocent little child!” Just then I saw—we all saw—another ghost take shape and become clear in the blue, misty light filling the hall. We had not seen her until now. It was another lady standing beside the old man, with a look of merciless hatred and triumphant scorn. She was very beautiful, with a soft white hat pulled down over her proud brows and a red, curling lip. She wore an open blue satin gown. I had seen that figure before. It was the image of Miss Furnivall in her youth. The terrible ghosts moved on, paying no attention to old Miss Furnivall’s desperate plea. The raised crutch fell on the little child’s right shoulder, while the younger sister watched, stony and deathly calm. At that moment, the dim lights and the fire that gave no heat went out by themselves. Miss Furnivall lay at our feet, struck down by a fatal paralysis.

Yes! They carried her to bed that night, and she never rose again. She lay facing the wall, muttering softly but constantly: “Oh! Oh! What is done in youth can never be undone in old age! What is done in youth can never be undone in old age!”
